metaData.title: RAG Never Dies: Zhang Yingfeng and the Obsession Hidden in Flow | Gravity
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article features an in-depth conversation with RAGFlow founder Zhang Yingfeng, exploring the evolution of RAG technology from product to infrastructure, the path to open-source commercialization, and the technological changes and entrepreneurial reflections brought about when RAG users shift from humans to agents.
metaData.summary: This article is a long-form interview with RAGFlow founder Zhang Yingfeng, part of CSDN's "Gravity" series. It begins with Zhang's personal journey, recounting his transition from a veteran in search technology to his first entrepreneurial venture, and details InfiniFlow's strategic pivot from developing the AI-native database Infinity to making RAGFlow its flagship product. The core discussion revolves around the present and future of RAG technology: Zhang firmly believes that "RAG is dead" is marketing rhetoric, asserting that retrieval itself is eternal. Especially in the age of agents, RAG users are shifting from humans to agents, fundamentally changing retrieval frequency, query length, and product form. The article also delves into the challenges of open-source commercialization, including long payment cycles and service-based payment models in the domestic market, as well as the strategic necessity of going global. It covers the technical decision to rewrite the online retrieval component of RAGFlow 1.0 in Go to boost performance. Additionally, Zhang shares the gains and losses of being a "veteran" entrepreneur, emphasizing adherence to core principles and a steadfast belief in long-term value.

mainPoints.point: "RAG is dead" is marketing rhetoric; retrieval is eternal.
mainPoints.explanation: Zhang Yingfeng believes that despite the emergence of technologies like ultra-long context windows, retrieval remains the core means for agents to acquire external knowledge and will not disappear. While RAG as a product form may become outdated, its underlying technology forms the foundation of an agent's data infrastructure.

mainPoints.point: RAG users are shifting from humans to agents, bringing fundamental changes.
mainPoints.explanation: Queries from agents are longer and more frequent (ranging from tens to thousands), requiring RAG systems to fully expose retrieval capabilities to agents, allowing them to autonomously decide on retrieval strategies. This drives the evolution of the RAG engine into a context engine.

mainPoints.point: The path to open-source commercialization is clear but requires patience in product refinement.
mainPoints.explanation: RAGFlow follows a path from open source to SaaS to on-premises deployment. In its early stages, due to limited manpower, the team prioritized product stability over rapid commercialization. The domestic market poses challenges such as long payment cycles and a tendency for enterprises to pay for services rather than products.

mainPoints.point: Going global is a necessity, not an option.
mainPoints.explanation: For Data Infra products, the overseas market is key to commercial success. Zhang plans to first launch a formal SaaS service, then decide on key deployment regions based on data feedback, and is prepared to physically relocate overseas if necessary.

mainPoints.point: RAGFlow 1.0 will rewrite the online retrieval component in Go to improve performance.
mainPoints.explanation: To handle the surge in retrieval requests in the agent era, the team is rewriting the online retrieval component from Python to Go to eliminate performance bottlenecks. Additionally, the 1.0 version marks product stability and production readiness.

keyQuotes: RAG is dead? Retrieval is eternal!
As a product form, RAG may not last long because RAG itself is essentially a simple agent. But retrieval itself is eternal.
A very important thing is happening now: the users of RAG are shifting from humans to agents.
Domestic companies may be willing to pay for products, but not necessarily in large numbers; they usually pay for services.
With AI coding, the value of humans is to serve as a safety net for these matters; only humans can provide that safety net.

relatedArticles.title: Dissecting OpenClaw: Understanding the Inner Workings of AI Agents
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: By analyzing the open-source project OpenClaw, this article reveals how AI Agents utilize system prompts, tool calling, memory management, and heartbeat mechanisms to transform simple "text completion" models into intelligent systems capable of autonomous task execution.

relatedArticles.title: From 7.9% to 54% Adoption: The Three-Stage Evolution of Kuaishou's Intelligent Code Review
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article details the three-generation architectural evolution of Kuaishou's intelligent code review system—from pure LLM heuristics to knowledge engine-driven, and finally to Agentic autonomous decision-making—increasing the CR adoption rate from 7.9% to 54%.

relatedArticles.title: Silicon Time's 10,000-Word Q&A (Part 1): The Disappearance of Code Illiteracy, the Rise of OPD, and Where the New Markets Are
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article, in a Q&A format, systematically explains the tiered transformation paths for programmers in the era of AI coding, the rise of OPD/OPC, the logic of application explosion driven by declining token costs, and four major new market opportunities, including the Agent marketplace.

relatedArticles.title: No More Blind Faith in Hackathons, We Completely Rebuilt the Agent 4 Times! Notion Leaders Reflect: How to Avoid 'Swimming Upstream' When Building AI Products?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article is compiled from a podcast interview with Sarah Sachs, Head of Notion AI Engineering, and Simon Last, Head of Product Prototyping. It provides an in-depth retrospective on Notion's winding journey of exploring and productizing AI Agents (Custom Agents) since 2022, sharing practical experience and core insights on technology selection, product design, team collaboration, and evaluation systems.

relatedArticles.title: RAG Optimization Dictionary: A Comprehensive Analysis of 20 RAG Optimization Methods
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically reviews and provides the principles, pros and cons, and Python implementations of 20 RAG optimization methods, covering full-link enhancement strategies from semantic chunking to Self-RAG.

relatedArticles.title: Deep Dive: The Memory Architecture and Philosophy That Thousands of Words Can't Fully Explain
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically constructs an architectural blueprint for AI Agent memory systems, proposing a System 2 architecture composed of raw ledgers, derived views, and control policies, aiming to achieve auditable, highly available, long-range personalized intelligence.

relatedArticles.title: 63-Year-Old Jensen Huang Adds Another Doctorate, Intel CEO Drapes His Robe, Latest Speech Goes Viral: The Era of Humans Writing Software and Computers Executing Instructions Is Over!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: In his commencement speech at CMU, Jensen Huang declared that the era of humans writing software and computers executing instructions is over, and that AI will bridge the technology gap, presenting unprecedented opportunities for graduates.

relatedArticles.title: RAG is Dead? No, Grep is Back!
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the leaked source code of Claude Code, this article deeply deconstructs its abandonment of RAG and vector retrieval in favor of an LLM-driven multi-round iterative Grep search mechanism. It compares this approach with Cursor and Codex, demonstrating the feasibility and design philosophy of a zero-index solution in code search scenarios.

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Former Meta Distinguished Engineer and current OpenAI Codex lead Michael Bolin shares the truth about big tech promotions, the culture shock of AI labs, and how AI is reshaping top engineers into 'code reviewers.'

relatedArticles.title: "Don't Rush to Fire the Bottom Rung—Maybe Executives Should Be the First to Get an AI Overhaul?"
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article is adapted from a conversation between Stay SaaSy and swyx, exploring management challenges brought by AI in organizations, including budget allocation, build vs buy decisions, code review risks, and the idea that executives should be the first to be AI-augmented.
